..
Issued at 1244 AM MDT Mon Aug 31 2026

I have arrived at work for another shift and for the first time
in a while the radar is clear, no showers in the county warning
area as drier air has spread across almost all of the area. 
However, the monsoon machine has been unrelenting this year, 
going almost nonstop for the last six to seven weeks with only 
a few stops for maintenance. We are in one of the those now, but
it won't last. The lock out / tag out on it will be removed 
later today and will again be fired up across the area tonight.

But today looks like a fairly nice start to the week for most, 
now the last day of August and of meteorological summer. After a
rather chilly start, with some frost possible in the deeper 
valleys in the west with temperatures dropping close to 
freezing, it should be comfortably warm this afternoon. 
Temperatures look to be fairly close to normal with light to 
moderate wind for most locations. The monsoonal moisture will 
begin to creep northward late today, with a few showers and 
thunderstorms south of roughly an Afton to Wamsutter line before
sunset. Moisture then spreads northward tonight, across much of
the area by sunrise. As for the potential of heavy rain and 
possible flooding, we once again have some factors in favor of 
it and some against it. Well above normal precipitable water 
values will again move across the area, as much as 175 percent 
of normal. The moisture will also be riding a shortwave lifting 
from the southwest, enhancing lift and mid level forcing. There 
are some factors against it as well. Most of the precipitation 
will fall at night, with limited surface instability and less of
a chance for thunderstorms. There will also be some mid level 
flow, so any showers or storms will not be stationary. At this 
point, the marginal risk of excessive rainfall looks reasonable 
for now, mainly in the west and south where the greatest lift 
will be. Chances of showers will continue into Tuesday as well, 
although chances of showers and heavy rain should decrease 
through the day as the deeper moisture moves away to the east. 
Most showers should end by midnight Tuesday night. As for 
amounts, most of the ensembles are giving at least a 2 in 3 
chance of a quarter of an inch or rain across most of the 
western mountains and valleys. The best chance of over a half an
inch or rain will be in the Wind River Range and Tetons with a 
greater than 1 out of 2 chance. Some locations will probably end
up with an inch of rain but with the nature of convection this 
is impossible to pinpoint.

Much drier air will the move across the area for the middle of the 
week as the moisture gets pushed to the east. However, we have 
another concern for these days. On these days, we will be between an 
upper level low over the Pacific Northwest and ridging over the 
southeast. The jet stream will also be nearby, as much as 90 knots, 
a decent speed for this time of year. The result will be a gusty 
wind developing across much of the area. Most areas will have at 
least a 3 out of 5 chance of wind gusts over 30 mph on Wednesday, 
Thursday and even into Friday. Some of the more wind prone areas 
could even see gusts to 50 mph, especially on Wednesday when the 
wind is expected to peak. The limiting factor will be humidity. The 
main area of concern looks to be East of the Divide where most 
locations have at least a 1 in 2 chance of relative humidity below 
15 percent. We will likely (around a 3 out of 4 chance) need 
some fire weather highlights for some if not much of the period.
It is still a bit too early right now though. And, we can't 
completely rule out a stray shower over the mountains but the 
chance is less than 1 out of 8 each day. Temperatures should be 
well above normal on these days, with the warmer spots, like the
eastern Bighorn Basin, having at least a 1 in 2 chance of 90 
degree highs each day.

The monsoon looks to make a return for next weekend as the ridge 
over the southeast retrogrades and moves back toward the southern 
plains. At the same time, an upper level low will be moving into the 
central Pacific coast. This may create a moist conveyor belt of 
moisture into the area for Saturday or Sunday with some possible
adding of moisture from a possible tropical storm or hurricane
off of the western Mexico coast. The GFS is very moist with 
precipitable water, showing around 200 percent of normal 
Saturday night into Sunday. This model does tend to run a bit 
hot on this, so reality is probably 20 to 25 percent less. 
However, the chance of showers and storms really increases on 
then. With the ridge remaining fairly stationary for a few days,
this pattern looks to continue into early next week. And with 
this, temperatures will remain above normal, generally around 7 
to 12 degrees above normal. So, the monsoon continues to stick 
around like an house guest that overstayed its welcome. However,
it will be leaving for a few days at least.
